condensed.text: Some places exist where animals almost never go because humans designed them for humans.
This story ends in such a place but starts in the opposite setting.
Dana Chivvis narrates the story.
The story begins in the rainforests of Indonesia on an island called Sulawesi.
Photographer David Slater traveled from England to Sulawesi a few years ago to photograph a troop of monkeys.
David spent a whole day following the monkeys through thick forest, tangles, vines, muddy undergrowth, cobwebs, and past poisonous snakes.
David found the experience of being like a monkey amazing and felt he had become one.
David had met monkeys all over the world before and understood monkey etiquette, including not showing teeth and not staring at their faces.
Making animals relaxed is one of the secrets to getting good wildlife photography.
David wanted to capture a full face portrait with a wide angle lens.
The monkeys looked away every time David approached taking the shot.
After two days of near misses, David changed his strategy.
David placed his camera on a tripod and threw down cookies to entice the monkeys over.
David hoped the monkeys would become curious about the camera and start pushing the button themselves.
The monkeys showed curiosity but did not push the button.
David attached a cable with a button on the end to the camera.
The monkeys liked the cable and started playing with it, putting it in their mouths and fighting over it.
When the monkeys pressed the button, they automatically looked into the lens.
The camera's clicking sound resembled monkey language.
The monkeys fired off a few shots.
David reviewed the photos and found them slightly out of focus but not bad.
David adjusted the camera settings and put the camera back.
The monkeys became very engaged with the project and grew too excited.
The monkeys almost knocked the tripod over.
David lay on his stomach and stretched his arm out to steady the tripod with two fingers.
Other monkeys noticed David lying on the floor and hopped onto his back.
David had monkeys on his back while trying to keep the camera steady as two or three monkeys played with the button.
David heard the camera going off.
David did not dare look up because he knew the monkeys would probably look away if he did.
David let the monkeys continue clicking the button.
David carefully looked up and saw the monkeys pulling amazing contorted faces with howling mouths and smiling expressions.
The monkeys took amazing, beautiful, and weird selfies.
David wanted the experience to continue forever.
David stood up and checked the photos, discovering the shots were exceptionally good selfies.
The photos transcended typical selfies and entered the realm of art.
One shot in particular caught David's eye.
The monkey's face appeared very close to the camera, looking straight into the lens with perfectly coiffed hair and friendly, big, round, amber eyes.
The selfie's main feature was the monkey's self-satisfied grin with oversized, gap-toothed teeth, appearing as if the monkey knew it was posing for a picture.
The narrator saw the image on the front cover of a publication like National Geographic and decided to send it to agents.
David and his agents released a press statement about the selfies to attract attention and promote conservation while also seeking to sell the pictures.
Crested black macaques are critically endangered, one step from extinction in the wild, having lost eighty percent of their population in forty years due to humans.
David traveled to Indonesia to photograph the monkeys and inspire humans to care about them and stop killing them.
The selfies did not appear on National Geographic's cover, but British tabloids showed interest, and the Daily Mail first published the story in 2011.
Within an hour the story spread across multiple countries including Australia and Germany, and David received overwhelming emails and phone calls from people wanting the story and image.
Over the following months David licensed the monkey selfies to publications and sold prints successfully.
One day David searched for crested black macaque on Google, found Wikipedia at the top of results, clicked it, and discovered his image there.
David wondered where Wikipedia obtained the image and whether they had paid a license fee to Caters News Agency.
They had not paid, so David sent Wikipedia a letter asking them to show a license or pay for the image.
Wikipedia replied that they believed the image was public domain, meaning anyone could use it without David's permission for free.
David considered this stealing because he earned his living selling pictures, and having a popular image was valuable to him.
Now anyone could download the image from Wikipedia and use it on their wall or in publications.
Wikipedia holds that internet information should be free and decided the selfie was public domain because the monkey pressed the button, making the monkey technically the creator.
Wikipedia assessed that monkeys cannot own copyrights, so the photo was free for all to use and belonged to the internet.
David felt baffled and believed he held the copyright because he set everything up, had intent and creativity, while the monkey only pressed the button.
Wikipedia included a note below the photo stating the file was public domain because a nonhuman animal created it and no human author held copyright.
Wikipedia's decision to declare the photo public domain started the monkey selfie legal battle.
Human nature with its laws, opinions, and domination displaced mother nature.
David assembled a legal team and studied copyright law.
David explored finding venture capitalists to fund a lawsuit against Wikipedia.
Wikimedia, the foundation owning Wikipedia, dismissed David at their London conference called Wikimania.
Co-founder Jimmy Wales attended the conference.
David learned that Jimmy Wales and conference delegates mocked him by printing his image on large boards throughout the facility.
Jimmy Wales and others encouraged delegates to take selfies with David's selfie image.
David found this behavior mean.
Multiple images of this mockery exist online, with the Jimmy Wales photo being particularly offensive to David.
The narrator searched online for images of Jimmy Wales with the monkey selfie.
A Google search for Jimmy Wales monkey selfie shows a photo of Wales holding his phone in one hand and the monkey selfie in the other while making a duck-face expression.
Neither speaker knew the origin of the duck-face pose, though many people make this expression.
David expressed feeling very angry when asked about seeing the Jimmy Wales selfie with his monkey photo.
David fought against a much larger opponent.
The battle escalated dramatically when a new massive challenge emerged.
The Wikimedia dispute had generated UK press coverage.
David's wife discovered online that a monkey was suing David as a photographer.
David learned about both Wikipedia using his image and the monkey lawsuit by stumbling across them online.
PETA helped the monkey from the selfie photos sue David for copyright infringement.
David called his lawyers and asked what he could do about the new development.
His lawyers told David the lawsuit appeared to be an April Fools joke and someone was pranking him.
The lawyers advised David to wait, not respond, and only worry if he received official legal papers.
The narrator confirmed the expectation.
One afternoon the narrator was at home when someone knocked at the door.
A man in a black suit stood on the porch.
The narrator opened the door and the man thrust a large A4-sized white envelope into the narrator's hand.
The man stated he had been instructed to deliver the documents.
The narrator asked what the documents were and opened the envelope in front of the man.
The narrator removed the contents and asked the man if he knew what they were.
The man said he did not really know.
The narrator told the man that a monkey was suing the narrator and showed him the documents.
The man started laughing and the two had a brief chat.
The man worked for a local firm nearby and then left.
Someone read the complaint and found it strange.

The complaint contained pages of copyright law legalese followed by exhibits consisting entirely of monkey selfies showing various expressions, resembling a legal document assembled by Curious George.
The monkey named Naruto sued David through his next friends, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals.
The official case name was Naruto, a Crested Macaque, by and through his Next Friends, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, Inc., versus David John Slater, an Individual.
In legal terminology, a next friend functions like a guardian who represents someone unable to represent themselves in court.
This arrangement resembles cases involving babies or disabled adults who cannot speak or represent themselves.
The narrator acknowledged understanding this concept, noting it is not unusual in human law.
PETA has a reputation for performing stunts to draw attention to animal welfare issues.
PETA once dumped horse manure outside Gordon Ramsay's London restaurant after a guest on his cooking show prepared a horse meat dish.
PETA created a comic book titled Your Mommy Kills Animals and distributed it to mothers wearing fur coats at Nutcracker performances.
PETA campaigned to rename fish as sea kittens so people would associate seafood with cats and stop eating fish.
Jeff Kerr, PETA's general counsel, stated the monkey selfie case was not a publicity stunt.
PETA first noticed the monkey selfie around 2014 when the dispute between Slater and Wikimedia became international news.
PETA immediately believed Naruto, as the photograph's creator, should own its copyright.
Jeff Kerr viewed the dispute as Slater wanting to sue Wikimedia while Wikimedia claimed the photo belonged to the public domain, with no one advocating for the monkey.
Kerr argued the law should apply equally to Naruto despite Naruto not being born human.
Someone noted the monkey certainly did not consciously intend to take photographs for purposes like updating a dating profile.
The monkey did not think of the act as taking a photograph.
Kerr argued copyright law does not require such intent and simply grants ownership to the author or creator of an image.
The law does not require the author to know they are making a photograph.
If someone hands over a camera and the recipient arranges subjects and takes a photograph, that person technically owns the copyright.
Someone joked about needing to sue French tourists who had taken photos for them.
PETA is an American organization.
The case was to be heard in federal court in San Francisco.
David consulted his lawyers in England, and they advised him to hire an American attorney and fight the case because otherwise the monkey might win.
David's advisors warned him that anything could happen in a California court and he could not take the risk.
David hired Andrew Dhuey to represent him.
Andrew first learned about the case by reading about it and became excited because the San Francisco federal court was near his Berkeley office.
Andrew is an intellectual property lawyer who works independently, and he reached out to David to ask if he could take the case.
Andrew believed he was perfect for the case because it lent itself to humor and monkey puns, which he enjoys.
Andrew uses a LinkedIn photo showing himself in a Chippendales costume wearing eyeglasses and a bow tie.
Andrew had practiced law for 25 years without being able to joke in court filings, and he saw this case as an opportunity to do so.
Andrew is a legitimate intellectual property lawyer who has defended the toy company WhamO and won an important case against Panasonic.
Andrew considered the case easy and filed a motion to dismiss Naruto's complaint, arguing that monkeys do not have standing to sue in federal court.
Andrew based his argument on the 2004 case Cetacean Community v George W. Bush, in which all the world's whales, porpoises, and dolphins sued the president.
The cetaceans argued that military underwater sonar was hurting them and changing their natural behaviors like eating and mating.
Sonar produces extremely loud sound waves, and cetaceans flee when they hear it, sometimes injuring themselves to escape.
The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in that case that animals do not have standing to sue in federal court unless Congress explicitly states otherwise.
Andrew pointed to that cetacean case in his defense.
PETA hired outside attorney David Schwarz from a prominent Los Angeles intellectual property law firm to represent the monkey Naruto in court.
Schwarz argued primarily that Naruto legally owned the copyright because he made the photo.
PETA also viewed the case as an opportunity to set precedent, disagreeing with the cetacean ruling and believing animals should have legal recourse in court.
A court clerk called civil matter 154324, Naruto v David John Slater, et al, and requested counsel to come forward and state their appearance.
This recording came from the hearing in the federal district court in San Francisco.
The judge asked Schwarz whether he had an example of an animal ever receiving a copyright in the history of common law.

Schwarz admitted he had no such example but argued that other humans were denied protection under that law due to their skin color, drawing a comparison to statutory interpretation problems in the antebellum period.
The judge interrupted and called that argument quite a stretch.
The narrator observes that Schwarz compared a monkey's lack of copyright to chattel slavery, which the narrator finds offensive and blind to the racist history of comparing black people to monkeys.
Schwarz appeared uncomfortable with his own argument, which equated denying a monkey property rights based on species to denying humans property rights based on skin color.
The judge repeated that the argument was quite a stretch, and Schwarz asked for clarification.
The judge confirmed the characterization but allowed Schwarz to continue.
Schwarz stated he would not make that argument his centerpiece but noted that before the 14th Amendment, property ownership concepts in patent law prevented slaves from claiming patent ownership.

PETA views the monkey selfie case within a larger strategy to get courts to recognize that denying animals property rights equals denying humans property rights, which would allow the legal system to reconsider the legal status of animals.
Courts would then declare animals as property owners rather than mere property.
PETA had previously attempted similar arguments in court, suing SeaWorld in 2011 on behalf of five orcas at SeaWorld Orlando and SeaWorld San Diego.
Orcas measure 20 to 30 feet long, weigh about six tons, and typically travel around 75 miles daily.
PETA argued that keeping these orcas in small concrete tanks against their will for human entertainment constituted slavery.
PETA lost that case, but SeaWorld agreed to end its captive orca program after its last 27 orcas die.
Understanding PETA's pursuit of such cases requires considering two different worldviews.

One worldview places humans at the top of the food chain because God willed it or because humans developed capabilities to hunt, gather, farm, build cities, and create copyright laws, making rules for everything else.
The other worldview, which PETA holds, positions humans not at the top but as just another mammal, meaning humans should extend their rights to fellow animals.
The narrator asked if PETA believes humans are not superior to other animals.
Jeff Kerr, PETA's general counsel, confirmed that humans are just another member of the animal kingdom and that prejudice and hubris prevent people from recognizing this.

Kerr described animals' property status as an abomination, stating that animals like Naruto are feeling, sentient beings who deserve fundamental legal rights beyond food, water, veterinary care, and shelter.
The idea that animals should have recognized fundamental legal rights has precedent.
Three years earlier in Argentina, a judge granted a habeas corpus petition on behalf of an orangutan held in a tiny, poor-quality cage at a Buenos Aires zoo.
The judge decided the orangutan had basic rights as a nonhuman person, including the right to freedom.
In New York state, an attorney fights to get courts to recognize two captive chimps, Tommy and Kiko, as nonhuman persons deserving legal rights similar to those corporations receive.
David Slater, the photographer whom the monkey is suing, agrees with PETA on this point.
David used to defend PETA to friends who grumbled about their stunts.
David once collaborated with PETA on a campaign to protect wild hogs near his home in England.
David expressed that PETA's greatest shame was attacking someone who shared their goals.
David stated that saving animals from suffering is noble but believed PETA sometimes gets carried away with their power.
An interviewer asked David whether PETA's opposition made him reconsider if they had a point.
David answered no.

David explained he had thought carefully about his philosophy because his Wildlife Personalities book, which was part of the court case, argued for animals having fundamental rights like dignity, access to ancestral forests, and access to food.
David identified himself as an animal rights advocate.
Naruto and PETA lost the first round in court.
Andrew Dhuey called David to tell him the news.
David and Dhuey reacted casually because they expected the case to be thrown out.
David noted that Andrew Dhuey had told him all along the case would not go anywhere.
PETA appealed on behalf of the monkey.
Attorney David Schwarz greeted the court and introduced himself as representing the appellant.
The case went before three judges on the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, the same court that had ruled against Trump's travel ban twice that year.
The narrator noted these judges were serious.
A judge interrupted Schwarz thirty seconds into his oral argument to pose a preliminary question.
At this stage the attorneys and judges debated case law, and the judges had many questions for Schwarz, beginning with how he qualified to be Naruto's next friend since he did not know the monkey.
A few minutes later Judge Randy Smith interrupted Schwarz to question him about injury, the legal term for harm or damage.

Judge Smith asked what injury existed, noting there was no way to acquire or hold money from copyright, no loss to reputation, and no allegation that the copyright could have benefited Naruto financially.

Schwarz began arguing redressability did not necessarily turn on compensation, but the judge interrupted to demand identification of the injury and stated no case established copyright infringement itself as injury.
The narrator remarked it was enjoyable hearing lawyers use terms like redressability, compensation, and injury while discussing a monkey.
The judge told Schwarz he would believe copyright infringement constituted injury if Schwarz provided supporting case law, but Schwarz had not done so, and the judge again asked what injury existed.
The judges and Schwarz debated case law, legal precedent, and the definition of author for twenty minutes before Andrew Dhuey took the floor.
After two years of research, legal filings, and oral arguments, Dhuey fulfilled his wish to make a monkey joke in court by saying monkey see monkey sue would not work in federal court.
Dhuey's remaining arguments essentially urged the court to dismiss the case and make PETA pay his legal fees.
Angela Dunning, the codefendant's attorney, stood up after Dhuey finished.
PETA had also sued the self-publishing book company that David had used.
Angela Dunning delivered a straightforward defense arguing that Naruto cannot benefit financially from his work because he is a monkey.
David Slater did not attend the court hearing in San Francisco because he did not want to spend money traveling from Wales to California.
David watched the entire hearing online.
David described watching three judges and the attorneys discussing monkeys, which made him realize he was being sued by a monkey.
Naruto did not attend the hearing and remained in the rainforest in Indonesia.
Nobody asked Naruto his opinion about the case.
After two years, the parties resolved the matter themselves and told the appellate court they no longer wanted a ruling.
In September, David and PETA announced they had reached a settlement with confidential details.
David Slater retained the monkey selfie copyright registered in his name in two countries.
David agreed to donate twenty-five percent of the photo proceeds to protect crested macaques.
Wikipedia continued displaying the monkey selfie for free download, claiming it was in the public domain.
David stated he would have to sue Wikipedia to remove the image and planned to do so.
Multiple monkeys were present when the selfies were taken that day.
PETA consulted a primatologist who works with crested black macaques, and she identified Naruto as the monkey in the famous selfie.
David disputed this identification, stating that Naruto is male but he remembers the monkey being female with a pink rump characteristic of female macaques.
The interviewer suggested Naruto was making a fraudulent claim, and David agreed that the wrong monkey appeared in court and took credit for work actually made by a female monkey.
David joked that feminists should protest and that this female monkey was probably not the first to have such an experience.
The narrator observed that both humans and monkeys naturally play in front of cameras, but only humans spend vast amounts of money and years in court over such matters.
Dana Chivvis produced the show, and the narrator announced that the next segment would feature a horse, continuing after a break from Chicago Public Radio.
The program is This American Life, hosted by Ira Glass.
Each week the program chooses a theme and presents different stories on that theme.
Today's show features stories about people attempting to completely erase the line between animal and human.
